newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Trade powers take India to WTO over import bars.
newsitem.headline: Trade powers take India to WTO over import bars.

text.p: The European Union is to join other trade powers in starting a case in the World Trade Organisation (WTO) against India's long-standing import restrictions, EU officials said on Thursday.

The move follows a similar decision earlier in the week by the United States, which has since been followed by Canada, Australia and New Zealand, all of whom argue the Indian measures run against WTO open trading accords.

Other developed countries and some former communist emerging economies in the trade body, which has been the scene of three unsuccessful rounds of negotiation on the issue this year, are expected to follow suit, diplomats said.

The restrictions, which affect some 2,700 items ranging from consumer goods to agricultural products, have been in force since the 1950s, but were accepted by other countries because of India's earlier endemic balance-of-payments (BOP) problems.
But with the steady growth in the country's foreign exchange reserves, which reached $28,8 billion in June, other WTO members have insisted that Delhi agree to move quickly to drop the curbs.
In June, India offered a phase-out over nine years and then cut the period to six years, but the big trading powers argued that this was too long.

The United States was reported pressing for a maximum of three years, while the EU and other WTO members were indicating readiness to accept five years if restrictions on most big-ticket items were removed early in the period.
A U.S. statement on Wednesday said WTO provisions allowed countries to impose measures like import surcharges and quantitative restrictions "to respond to a legitimate balance of payments crisis.

"India has maintained import restrictions imposed on BOP grounds for decades. However, under current circumstances, India no longer meets WTO criteria for use of BOP provisions, thus the measures currently in place are no longer justified," it added.
Trade diplomats said the argumentation in documents filed with the WTO by the other complainants notifying the body of their own requests for consultations with India was almost identical.
Analysts in Delhi said earlier this month it was likely that India would now propose a five-year phase-out, but there has been no formal word from the Indian government.
Under the WTO's dispute settlement procedure, India has to respond to the requests for consultations within 10 days and start them within 20 days.

If after two months no solution is in sight, the complaining powers can ask the WTO's Dispute Settlement Body to set up a panel to rule on the issue. But some have said they would not like the problem to go that far.

Australia's Deputy Prime Minister Tim Fischer said on Wednesday that although the restrictions were denying his country's exporters fair access to the Indian market, he hoped for an early settlement through consultations.
